activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.
story:
Scarlett was playing in the yard with Baani. They rolled a red ball down the hill. The ball stopped by the fence.

Scarlett ran to get it. Then she saw something small on the grass. It was a little stick with a button. It looked like a lighter.

Baani came over. "What is that?" she asked.

"I think it's a lighter," said Scarlett. She did not pick it up. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," she said.

"Let's go tell a grown-up," said Baani.

They ran to Scarlett's dad. He was watering the flowers. Scarlett held his hand and showed him the fence. Dad picked up the lighter and put it in his pocket. "Good job, girls," he said.

The sun went down. The ball went back in the toy box. Scarlett got tired and went to her bed. Dad tucked her in. "Night night, Scarlett," he said. She smiled and closed her eyes.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread.
story:
Charlie stood in the kitchen. The toast was on her plate. Her dad had made it hot, and now it was cool enough to touch.

"You can try the butter," her dad said. He gave her a small knife with a dull edge. He stayed right beside her. Charlie held the knife. She poked the toast with the tip. The toast got a hole in it. Butter went on in one big lump. "Why did that happen?" she asked. Her dad said, "Try the flat side. Watch what it does."

Charlie turned the knife over. She laid the flat side on the butter. Then she pushed it across the bread. The butter spread out thin. The whole toast turned yellow. "Look!" said Charlie. "One push, then two, then three." She counted her pushes. Three pushes made it smooth.

Next came the milk. Charlie held the cup with both hands. She poured slowly. The milk went up the side, one inch, then two. Not one drop spilled. There was a flower on her cup, and now the flower looked like it was swimming. "Can I make more toast tomorrow?" she asked. Her dad smiled and said, "Yes, butter girl."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
story:
Emilia went to the store with her dad. She wanted to pick a present for her grandma. Near the bread, there was a little play spot. Saanjh from her class was there. He was building a tall block tower.

Emilia ran over fast. Her elbow bumped the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. All of them. Saanjh's mouth went wobbly. "My tower," he said.

Emilia felt hot in her face. She took a big, deep breath. "Sorry, Saanjh," she said. "I bumped your tower." Then she got down on her knees. She put one block on the bottom. Then another. Saanjh put the top block on. The tower stood tall again.

Saanjh smiled at her. Emilia smiled back. She held her dad's hand. "Present time," she said, and off they went to the card aisle.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
story:
Andrew went to the park with his mom. They walked past the swings first. The slide was long and silver. Andrew slid down, down, down. The metal felt cold under his hands. "Nice sliding," said his friend Axton.

Then they went to the little farm stand by the gate. A snowy white pig lived there. Andrew patted the pig with one finger. The pig made a happy oink. But then Andrew looked around. He could not see his mom. Too many people. His tummy felt tight.

Andrew remembered something. He saw a lady at the stand with a big red vest. She had a cash box. She worked there. Andrew walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The lady held his hand. "Let's look together," she said. They stepped past the pig, past the swings. There was Mom, right by the slide. Mom hugged him tight. "You found a helper," Mom said. "I did," said Andrew, and he waved to the lady in red.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help.
story:
Joshua was in bed. The room was dark. Then he heard a noise. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window.

Joshua felt scared. He pulled the blanket up. The noise came again. Tap, tap. His tummy felt tight.

Joshua got out of bed. He went to Mommy's room. "I heard a noise," he said. "I feel scared."

Mommy took his hand. Her hand was warm and soft. "Come on," she said. "We can look together."

They walked down the hall. Mommy turned on the light. The room felt less dark. Then they heard the noise again. Tap, tap.

Mommy opened the curtain. A tree branch was tapping the glass. The wind was moving it. "That is a cool branch," said Joshua. He was not scared now.

They saw Grandpa's dog outside in his bed. The dog heard them and began to bark. "Woof!" he said.

Mommy tucked Joshua back into bed. The blanket smelled like clean laundry. "If you feel scared again, you can tell me," she said. "I will help you."

Joshua closed his eyes. Tap, tap, went the branch. He smiled and went to sleep.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
story:
Avery sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. "Where are we going now?" she asked. Mom said, "To the park. Today we play at the park." Avery clapped her hands. She wanted to see the ducks.

At the park, Avery found her friend Gwendolyn. Gwendolyn was throwing thin little sticks into the pond. "I came to this park tomorrow," said Gwendolyn. Then she stopped. She put one ear toward Avery. "No, wait. Yesterday. I came yesterday." Avery blinked. Yesterday was the day already done. Tomorrow was the day not here yet.

"I want to do that too," said Avery. She picked up a thin stick. She threw it in the water. A duck swam fast to the stick. Splash! "Look! My stick made the duck come!" said Avery. Gwendolyn threw her stick too. Another duck came. Two ducks, two sticks.

"Now it is time to go home," said Mom. Avery waved to the ducks. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Yes. Tomorrow we will come back." In the car, Avery looked out the window. "Bye, park," she said. "See you tomorrow."

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: In a drawing app, moving your finger across the screen draws a line.
story:
Myles went to his mom's office. The office was on a busy street. Myles saw a tablet on the desk. "Can I use it?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Let me turn it on for you." She pressed the button. The screen lit up. Mom tapped a drawing app. "You can draw," she said. Then she went back to work.

Myles looked at the big white screen. He moved his finger across the screen. A green line followed his finger! He moved his finger again. More lines, like squiggles. Then he stopped. The squiggly line looked like a snake. "A snake!" said Myles. He drew one eye. He drew a long tail. His friend Logan came by with his own mom. "Wow," said Logan. "Draw another one!"

Myles drew two more snakes. His finger got tired. "All done," he said. He pressed the button like Mom did. The screen went dark. He folded his hands in his lap. "I put it away," he said. Mom smiled. "Good job, Myles." Logan waved goodbye. Myles waved back and held his mom's hand.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Pouring slowly helps keep milk from splashing out of the cup.
story:
Lily stood in the restaurant kitchen with her dad. The cook, Mr. Wright, made hot toast on the big stove. "Can I help?" Lily asked. "You can spread the butter," said her dad. Lily took the knife. He helped her hold it. She spread the soft butter. The toast turned shiny and yellow.

"Now the milk," said Mr. Wright. He set a cup on the table. Lily picked up the jug. She poured fast. Milk splashed out onto the table. "Oh no," said Lily. Her dad wiped the table. "Try again," he said kindly. He gave her a new cup. This time Lily poured slowly. The milk went in, and not one drop came out. The cup was high and full.

Lily carried the cup with two hands. She set it by the toast. "Look, Dad!" she said. Dad smiled at her. Lily drank some milk and ate her buttery toast. "More toast, please?" she asked. Mr. Wright laughed and gave her a slice.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.
story:
Jaxson wanted to bake cookies with his dad. His tummy was hungry for warm cookies. First they had to shop for butter and sugar. Jaxson helped carry the small bag home.

In the kitchen, Dad turned on the oven. "The oven is hot," Dad said. Jaxson stayed back and watched. Dad mixed the dough. Jaxson helped stir. He was not lazy about stirring. He stirred and stirred.

Then Jaxson moved the chair to reach the counter. He saw a little hole in the wall. It was an outlet. He wanted to put his finger in it. "Dad, look at this hole," Jaxson said. Dad came right over. "That hole is an outlet," Dad said. "Never put fingers or things into it." Jaxson nodded. He kept his fingers on the spoon instead.

The cookies went into the hot oven. Only Dad touched the oven. Jaxson waited by the table. Soon the cookies were done. "You kept everyone safe today," Dad said. Jaxson took a big bite of his warm cookie.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: The last number you say when counting tells how many there are altogether.
story:
Sienna ran into the community centre. It was a sunny day after a stormy summer morning. Mr. Hassan had a big box of crayons.

"Let's count!" said Mr. Hassan. He put crayons on the table. He put four crayons in one pile. He put two crayons in another pile.

Sienna pointed at the piles. "Which pile has more?" asked Mr. Hassan. Sienna counted the big pile. "One, two, three, four." She jumped up and down. "Four! The last number was four!"

Benjamin counted the small pile. "One, two. Two!" he said.

"Four is more than two!" said Sienna. She hugged the big pile of crayons.

"You can use them all," said Mr. Hassan. Sienna drew a big sun. Benjamin drew a stormy cloud with rain.

Jenny came over. "How many pictures?" she asked. Sienna counted. "One, two. Two pictures!"

"Two crayons each," said Sienna, and she shared them out.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Later means some time after now, not right away.
story:
Daniel sat in his car seat. He held his red doll tight. "Are we at Grandma's now?" he asked. "Not now," said Dad. "Later." Daniel looked out the window. One cow. Two cows. Three cows. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "No, not yet," said Dad. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Daniel watched the trees go by. Yesterday he played with Antonio. Today he was in the car. Tomorrow he would see Grandma again. "Is it later now?" he asked. Dad laughed. "Almost! Count the cows for me." Daniel counted. One more cow. Two more cows.

Then the car slowed down. Dad did not pull into a farm. He pulled into Grandma's driveway. Her door opened. "Now it is later!" said Daniel. Grandma waved. "Come here, little one!" Daniel hugged his doll and ran to her.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Things can end up inside other things, like a toy tucked in a bag or coat pocket.
story:
Hazel went to the grocery store with her dad. She held her little bunny toy. Then she let go to help pick apples. When they walked on, her hands were empty.

"Where is Bunny?" Hazel asked. She looked by the apples. She looked under the cart. She looked at the bread. No bunny.

Mr. Sánchez worked at the store. "Let me help you look," he said. They walked slowly past the milk and the lake of spilled peas nobody had swept yet. Then Hazel stopped.

She looked at her dad's big coat pocket. The pocket was bumpy. Bunny could be inside a pocket! She reached in. Out came Bunny, soft and warm.

"Bunny was hiding in your pocket, Daddy," Hazel said. Dad laughed and hugged her. At home, Hazel put Bunny in her own pocket. Then she ran outside to play.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: In Japan, people say 'itadakimasu' before eating to give thanks for the food.
story:
Aiden ran into the community hall. His boots went clomp, clomp, clomp. Hiba and Daksh were already at the little table. Ms. Iyer was setting out rice and warm soup. Aiden was very hungry.

"Before we eat, we say a special word," said Hiba. "My grandma taught me. In Japan, people say 'itadakimasu' before eating. It gives thanks for the food." Aiden opened his mouth. "Itchy donkey mouse!" he said. Daksh laughed and laughed. "That is not it! Not it at all!"

Aiden tried again. "Ita... daki... masu." Hiba clapped. "Almost! Say it with me. Itadakimasu!" They all said it together. "Itadakimasu!" Then Ms. Iyer put the food on the table. Aiden took a big bite of rice. "Yum," he said. "I said the true word, and now I can eat!" He wiggled his boots under the table. "Itadakimasu," he whispered to his bowl. "Thank you, rice."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Covering different holes on a recorder makes different notes.
story:
Maya ran into the garage with her recorder. Travis was already there, waiting by the big blue bag of toys. "Listen to this!" said Maya. She blew into her recorder. It made a loud squeak. Travis covered his ears.

"That was a bad sound," said Travis. Maya looked at her recorder. She saw the little holes on top. She tried again. One finger was not covering its hole all the way. She pressed that finger down hard. She blew. Now the recorder sang a real note.

"It works!" Maya shouted. She lifted her finger off the hole. She blew again. A different note came out. She put it back. The first note came back. Travis laughed. "Let me try!" he said. He pressed all the holes down hard. His recorder sang too. The two friends played their notes together, loud and happy.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read.
story:
Lily sat in the reading corner. She hugged a big red book. It was about a dragon who could not fly. She loved every page.

"You have to put it back now," said Isha. "The book lives here."

Lily did not want to put it back. Her lip went down, down, down.

Ms. Buchanan came over. She held out a small card. It was blue with Lily's own name on it. "This is a library card," she said. "A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read."

Lily's eyes went big. "Even the dragon book?"

"Even the dragon book."

Ms. Buchanan zapped the card on her desk. Beep! Then she zapped the book. Beep! "Now it can go home with you."

Lily held the book tight. The cover felt rough under her fingers. "Come on, dragon," she said. "You can hang out at my house."

Isha giggled. "The dragon sleeps at your house tonight!"

"He snores," said Lily. "You will hear it tomorrow."

At the door, Lily waved the blue card high. "See you soon, library!" she called.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A plant's roots grow down into the soil.
story:
Blake went to the garden center with her dad. She picked out small tomato plants. "We will plant them at home," said Dad. Blake held a plant in her little hands.

At home, Blake dug a hole in the dirt. Then she saw a weed. She pulled it up. "Whoa!" said Blake. Long stringy roots hung down from the weed. Her friend Rocco came to play. "Look at the strings!" he said. "Those are roots," said Dad. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

So Blake put her tomato plant in the hole. She made sure the roots went down into the dirt. She patted the soil on top. Every day she gave it water. After some days, small green tomatoes grew. "A big number of tomatoes!" said Blake. Rocco laughed. "Can we taste one?" he asked. Dad smiled and picked one red tomato for them.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Peas grow inside pods on the plant.
story:
Sophie dug a little hole at the community garden. Ms. Kim handed her pea seeds. "Drop them in," said Ms. Kim. Sophie dropped them and patted the dirt. Every day she came back with her watering can. Green shoots popped up. Then tall vines grew. Sophie watered and watered, but she saw no peas anywhere. "Where are my peas?" she asked. "I don't see them!"

Paris came over to look. He picked a long green pod. "Is this a bean?" he asked. Sophie was worried. Was it the wrong plant? Ms. Kim smiled. "Open it and see," she said. Sophie pressed the pod with her thumb. It popped open. Inside lay a neat row of little round peas, like green beads.

"Peas!" Sophie shouted. "They grow inside the pod!" She picked pod after pod and filled her basket. She gave one to Paris and one to Marion, who was watering the carrots. A pig puppet sat on the fence post, and Sophie made it sniff the pods. It was getting late, so Ms. Kim said, "Time to go home." Sophie held her basket tight. "We can eat these at dinner," she said.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A new baby must be touched very gently.
story:
Logan ran into the baby store. "The baby needs things!" he said. Mom said, "We need a cozy blanket." Logan followed her down the big aisle. He saw tiny shoes. He saw tiny socks. He saw a little bed with soft sides.

Then Logan saw something wonderful. His friend Sehaj was there too! Sehaj held a demo baby doll. "My mom has a real baby at home," Sehaj said. Logan patted the doll's head. Pat, pat, pat! He patted hard. Sehaj's eyes got big. "Too hard!" Sehaj said. "The baby is little. A new baby must be touched very gently."

Logan tried again. He stroked the doll's tiny hand. Soft, soft, soft. The doll's hand wiggled, just a little. "It moved!" Logan said. Sehaj smiled. "Gentle hands make the baby happy," he said.

Mom held up two cozy blankets. "Pick one, Logan." Logan picked the blue one with stars. At home, the real baby lay in the crib. Logan reached out slowly. He stroked the baby's hand, soft, soft, soft. The baby's tiny fingers curled around Logan's finger and held on. Logan laughed. "She likes gentle hands!" he said. "Hello, baby. I am Logan."

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: You open your mouth wide so the dentist can see every tooth.
story:
Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. His dad was driving to the dentist. It was Brooks's first time going. A big plane flew over the car. Brooks watched it zoom away. He felt a little worried.

"I will sit still," said Brooks. "But what do I do with my mouth?"

His dad smiled. "You open your mouth wide so the dentist can see every tooth," he said.

At the dentist, Brooks sat in a big chair. The dentist said, "Say hello, Brooks." Brooks closed his mouth to talk. The dentist could not see any teeth then. Brooks tried again. He opened his mouth wide, like a lion's roar. Now the dentist could see every tooth.

"Very nice teeth!" said the dentist. Brooks got a sticker of a plane. He jumped down from the chair. "I want to come back!" he said.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed.
story:
Levi's class had a big basket. It sat by the cubbies at school. Levi put his muddy socks on the floor. He wanted to play, not clean.

His friend Ahaan picked up a sock. "Watch this," Ahaan said. He tossed the sock. It went into the basket. Swish! Levi laughed loud. "My turn!" said Levi.

Levi lifted his other sock. He threw it. It hit the edge and fell out. Sasha giggled. "Try again," she said. Levi tried again. This time it went in. Swish! "Basket!" he shouted.

Ms. Wijaya clapped her hands. "Good work," she said. "Now those dirty socks can get washed." Levi felt proud. He gave the basket a gentle pat, like a hug.

The next day, Levi wore his clean socks. They smelled like flowers. He wiggled his toes inside his shoes. "My socks got washed!" he told Sasha. She wiggled her toes too. At play time, Levi aimed one more sock. Swish! Right into the basket.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Feelings change, so a sad feeling can turn into a happy one later.
story:
Gabriel wanted to go to the park. He held his red ball by the door. Then the sky turned dark. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap.

"No park today," said his mom. "We need to stay inside."

Gabriel felt sad. His lip went down. His eyes felt watery. He sat on the floor and hugged his ball.

Then his mom brought a big blanket. "We can build a fort," she said. Gabriel jumped up. He felt excited now!

They put chairs together. They spread the blanket on top. Gabriel crawled inside. It was cozy and dark. His mom gave him a little flashlight.

"Wow," said Gabriel. "My fort!"

He shined the light on the red ball. The ball glowed inside the fort. Gabriel laughed and laughed.

Just then the phone rang. It was Iqra from school. "Come to my house tomorrow," she said. "We can play at the park together."

"Okay!" said Gabriel. He was happy.

The rain still tapped outside. But inside the fort, Gabriel smiled. He gave his mom a big hug through the blanket door.

The rain tapped, and Gabriel laughed.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Toys cannot really feel, but you can pretend they do.
story:
Benjamin was at daycare. He dropped his teddy bear on the floor. The bear went bump on the tiles.

Benjamin felt scared. "Is my bear hurt?" he asked.

Ms. Baptiste picked up the bear. She gave it a big hug. "The bear cannot really feel," she said. "But you can pretend it does."

Benjamin hugged the bear too. He patted its head. He made a little bed from a scarf.

Jasmine came over with her doll. "My doll is hungry," she said.

"Pretend it can eat," said Benjamin. He held a toy cup to the doll's mouth. Jasmine made slurp sounds. Then they built a pretend mountain of soft blocks. The doll climbed to the top.

"More soup, please," Jasmine said in a tiny doll voice. Benjamin laughed and poured again.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Day and night are opposites.
story:
Clara lay on her little mat at school. One mat, one blanket, one bear. She closed her eyes for rest time. The room went very quiet. Then it went very dark.

Clara woke up and opened her eyes. She could not see the sun. She could not see the blocks or the easel. She saw only black. "It is morning," she said. "Time to play!" She stood up fast and bumped her toe. "Ow," she said, and sat down slow.

Mr. Moretti came over with a small lamp. He helped her look out the big window. "The sky is dark," he said. "It is night, not day." Paige was awake too, holding her bird with one paper wing. "Night and day are opposites," said Paige. "Night is dark. Day is bright." Clara held her bear and watched the wild wind move the tree.

Mr. Moretti brought warm milk. First it was too hot, so Clara waited. Then it was just right, not hot, not cold. She took small sips. One sip, two sips, three. Outside, a car went by fast. Then all was slow and still again. The lamp made a little circle of light on the floor.

Clara looked out at the dark sky one more time. "Night," she whispered to her bear. Then she lay back down. One mat, one blanket, one bear. She closed her eyes and waited for day.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut to remember it.
story:
Miles sat in the family car. His hair was wet from a quick bath. Today he would get his first haircut at a salon. "I want to look like Dad," he said.

At the salon, the hairdresser put a blanket around Miles. Snip, snip went the scissors. A little curl fell down. The hairdresser was careful, and Miles sat very still.

Then Dad picked up the little curl. He put it in a small envelope. "Why?" asked Miles. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut," said Dad. "We keep it to remember this day."

Back in the car, Miles held the envelope. He saw one small curl. Now it sat in paper, saved. "I want to see it at home," said Miles. Dad smiled and buckled him in.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, lion dancers move to the beat of loud drums.
story:
Lillian went to the cultural center with her dad. There were red lanterns on the wall. Edmund and Asees were there too. "Come look!" said Edmund.

Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! They were very noisy. Lillian put her hands on her ears. "Too loud," she said. A big lion came out. It was gold and red. The lion jumped and shook its head.

Asees clapped her hands. "Watch the lion," she said. Lillian looked. The drums went boom, and the lion jumped. The drums went boom again, and the lion jumped again. The lion moved to the beat of the loud drums! Lillian let go of her ears. She clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. The lion danced faster, and Lillian clapped faster. "The lion hears the drums!" she said. Mr. Russo smiled and gave her a little red paper lantern. Lillian held it up high and clapped one more time.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
story:
Billie stood in the bakery kitchen with her mom. The oven door was open. It was hot inside. "Can I touch it?" Billie asked. "No, it needs a grown-up," her mom said. "You stay back here."

The kitchen lights were bright. A big door swung open and shut. Billie peeked through it. There were shelves and shelves of bread. She walked a little way. Then a little more. She turned around. She could not see her mom.

Billie looked and looked. Her tummy felt small. Then she saw the checkout counter. A worker stood there with a red apron. Billie walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," she said. "Can you help me?" "Yes, I can," the worker said. She held Billie's hand and called out. Mom came running from the kitchen door. She hugged Billie tight. "You told the store worker," Mom said. "That was just right." Billie smiled and held on all the way to the car.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.
story:
Hayden wanted to wash his hands. He stood on his step stool by the sink. His toy lion sat on the edge, watching him. "You wait there," Hayden told the lion.

Dad turned the tap. "Hot water is for me," said Dad. "Cold water is for you." The cold water ran over Hayden's hands. It felt cool and nice.

Then Hayden saw something small and red by the soap. It looked like a little candy. He wanted to pick it up. But he stopped. He kept his hands in the water. "Dad, there is a candy," he said.

Dad looked. "That is not candy. That is medicine. Only a grown-up gives you medicine." Dad picked it up and put it away high in the cabinet. Hayden washed and washed, slow and careful. He dried his hands all by himself.

Dad clapped. Hayden hugged his lion. "You are special," he whispered.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: In English, the words on a page are read from left to right.
story:
Edouard wanted to find the dog page in the book corner. The book was big and red. He sat on the soft rug and opened the cover. The pages felt smooth and cool. "Where is the dog?" he asked. "I will look and look," he said.

He put his finger at the right side of the page. He slid it left to left, back to the front of the line. His friend Amiyah came to sit with him. "One page, two pages, three pages," they counted together. But no dog.

Ms. Liu knelt down beside them. "Start here," she said. She pointed to the left side of the page. Edouard put his finger there. He slid it from left to right, word by word. "One word, two words, three words," he said. Then he turned to the next page. Then the next.

There it was. A big brown dog with a tight red collar. "A pet dog!" said Edouard. He patted the picture with his hand. The dog looked soft. Amiyah laughed and clapped. Edouard turned one more page, from the front of the book to the back. "Good dog," he said. "Good book."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes.
story:
The wind blew hard at the park. Riley held her hair with both hands. Sand flew up from the sandbox. "Ow," said her friend Salem. "Something went in my eye!" He blinked and blinked. A bit of dirt fell out on his cheek.

Riley blinked too. She blinked fast, like a butterfly. Nothing went into her eyes. "How come?" she wondered. She looked at Salem's face. He had little hairs above his eyes. She had them too. She could feel them when she touched her eyelids, soft as a feather.

Riley sniffed the air with her nose. She smelled popcorn. She heard the popcorn cart, boom, boom, going over the bumps. "I hear it with my ears!" she said. Ms. Reddy, her neighbour, was buying a bag. She gave Riley one warm piece. Riley tasted the salt on her tongue. Yum.

Then a big gust of wind came. Sand flew everywhere. Riley shut her eyes tight. She felt her little hairs stand out like a fence. When she opened her eyes, they felt fine. No dirt inside. "The sand stopped at my lashes," she said. Salem leaned close and looked. "My hairs stopped it too," he said. "Our eyes stayed clean!" Ms. Reddy smiled and held out the popcorn bag for one more piece.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Each arm goes into its own sleeve of the coat.
story:
Hailey was at the grocery store with her dad. It was cold outside. Hailey wanted to wear her red coat. "Can I put it on all by myself?" she asked. "Yes, you can," said her dad.

Hailey sat down on the bench. She pushed one arm into one sleeve. Then she pushed her other arm in too. But it went into the same sleeve! Both arms were stuck in one sleeve. "Look, I am a one-arm snake!" she said. Her dad laughed. A lady with carrots laughed too.

"Where does my other arm go?" Hailey asked. She wiggled her arm and looked. The other sleeve was empty. So she pulled her arm out. She put one arm in this sleeve. She put her other arm in that sleeve. One arm in each sleeve. The coat sat just right on her!

Now the zipper. Hailey pulled it up, up, up. Click, it closed at the top. "I did it!" she said. Her dad gave her a big smile. Outside, snow was starting to fall. Hailey stuck out her tongue to drink a snowflake. It was cold and tiny. "Snow is true," she said, and they walked to the car.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes loud sounds quieter.
story:
Emmett woke up from his nap. He was hungry. He ran to the kitchen. His dad was there, and so was the big blender.

Emmett looked at it with his eyes. He touched the cold counter with his hands. He sniffed with his nose. "I smell strawberries," he said.

"I smell them too," said Dad. "Smoothie time."

Then Dad turned the blender on. Whirrrr! It was so loud. Emmett's ears hurt. He put his hands right over his ears. The loud sound got quiet, just like that.

Emmett tried it. Ears open. Whirrr! Ears covered. Quiet. "Dad! My hands make it quiet!" he said.

"That is a good trick," said Dad. "One, two, three, four, five. Count your fingers over your ears." Emmett counted. One, two, three, four, five.

The blender stopped. Emmett took a taste of the smoothie with his tongue. "Yum," he said. "Can we sweep the crumbs too?"

"Sweep later," said Dad. "First, drink your wild pink drink."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: It is hard to see in the dark, so we turn on a light.
story:
Everett sat at the dinner table. He sniffed with his nose. "Mmm, soup!" he said. He touched his cup. It felt rough on the side. He tapped it. Tink, tink! He heard the sound with his ears.

Then Everett looked down. His teddy was gone! "Where is Ted?" he cried. He ran to his room. The room was dark. He could not see Ted anywhere. He froze like a statue.

"I can't see in the dark!" said Everett. His dad came in. Dad turned on the lamp. Click! The room filled with light. There was Ted, under the bed. Everett grabbed him and hugged him tight. He kissed Ted's soft ear. "Found you!" he said.

Back at the table, Everett took a big bite of soup. "Yum! I taste carrots," he said. Dad laughed. "You used your tongue, too! What a busy summer day for your eyes, ears, nose, hands and mouth."

"Taste it, Ted," said Everett. He held the teddy up to the bowl. "Ted says it tastes like carrots," he whispered. Dad smiled and gave him one more spoonful.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: Holding onto the edge of the pool, children can practice kicking their legs.
story:
Logan stood by the big hotel pool. The water was blue and shiny. His dad held his hand. Logan wanted to swim like the big kids. But the water looked deep. He felt a little scared.

His dad said, "Hold the edge, Logan." Logan put his small hands on the cool wall. Then his dad said, "Kick your legs." Logan kicked and kicked. His legs made big splashes. The splashes were white and cold on his chin. He kicked so hard, water flew up and hit Mr. Esposito, the pool teacher. "Splash!" said Mr. Esposito, laughing and wiping his face. Logan laughed too. He was not scared anymore. He held on tight and kept kicking.

Then his dad picked him up. "You did it," his dad said. Logan looked at his cute yellow float toy bobbing in the water. "Kick more tomorrow?" he asked. His dad hugged him with a warm, soft towel. "Yes," he said. "Kick more tomorrow."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After a visit ends, families can stay in touch with phone calls, video calls or letters.
story:
Grandma came to stay at Jaxon's house. She stayed for a whole week. They played in the backyard every day. They dug in the dirt. A long snake lay in the sun. "Is the snake afraid of us?" Jaxon asked. "No," said Grandma. "It slides away because we are big."

Then the week was done. Grandma packed her bag. She waved and drove away. Jaxon felt sad. He sat on the back step.

"What can we do now?" he asked his dad. "We can call her," said Dad. "On the phone?" asked Jaxon. "Yes. We can hear her voice." Jaxon called Grandma. He heard her say hello. The next day they made a video call. Jaxon saw her face on the screen. Then Jaxon drew a snake in the sun. Dad put the picture in an envelope. It was a letter for Grandma. Jaxon ran to the mailbox with it.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Small children sometimes sit on a booster seat so the hairdresser can reach their hair.
story:
Sienna was at Grandma's house. Grandma said, "Time for your first haircut!" Sienna patted her curls. "My hair is big like a mountain," she said. Grandma laughed. "Off we go."

At the salon, there was a big chair. Sienna climbed up. But she was small. The hairdresser bent down low. She bent lower and lower. "I cannot reach your hair," she said. Sienna thought hard. Then the hairdresser brought a booster seat. "Small children sit on a booster seat," she said, "so I can reach." The booster seat went on the big chair. Sienna sat on it. Now she was up, up, up!

"Now I can reach your hair," said the hairdresser. Snip, snip, snip. The curls fell like soft little pieces. "Snip, snip, snip!" said Sienna. Grandma held up the mirror. "Look at you!" Sienna grinned. "Grandma, do you need a booster seat too?" Grandma laughed and laughed. "Not yet," she said. Sienna hugged her tight. "Maybe tomorrow!"

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: It is a good habit to wash your hands after touching a pet or cleaning its cage.
story:
Oliver walked home with a small cage. Inside was a white rabbit. "His name is Snowy," said his dad.

At home, Oliver fed Snowy a carrot. He cleaned the cage with his dad. Snowy had soft fur. Oliver patted him a lot.

Then Oliver ran to the kitchen. He wanted his crackers. His mom stopped him at the door. "Wash your hands first," she said. "You touched Snowy and his cage." Oliver looked at his hands. He could not see anything on them.

Oliver washed his hands with soap. The water felt nice and warm. Then he ate his crackers.

The next day, Elijah came over. Elijah patted Snowy too. Then Elijah ran to the snack plate. Oliver called, "Wait! Wash your hands first." Elijah washed his hands. Then they shared the crackers and laughed.

"Snowy is a good rabbit," said Oliver. He gave Snowy one more gentle pat.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a game, players often tell the other team "good game."
story:
Cooper ran onto the soccer field. The grass was still wet. His red shirt felt bright in the sun. His friend Jolene ran beside him. She kicked the ball to him. Cooper kicked it back. The coach blew the whistle.

The other team scored a goal. Then they scored one more. The whistle blew again. The game was over. Cooper's team had lost. He sat down on the grass. He did not want to talk. His face felt hot. Jolene sat next to him. "We lost," he said.

Mr. Kaya clapped his hands. "Line up, everyone," he said. "We say good game to the other team." Cooper stood in the line. Each player walked past. Each player said, "Good game." A boy from the other team said, "Good game, Cooper." Cooper said it back. Then a small surprise. The boy smiled and held out his hand for a high five. Cooper laughed and clapped it. Jolene took a drink of water. "Good game," she said again. "Good game," said Cooper. The sky was turning pretty and pink.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Paintbrushes are washed with water and left to dry when painting is finished.
story:
Rosalie ran into the art room. Big paper waited on the table. Mr. Castillo held up a jar of paint. "This is red," he said. "Say it with me!" "Red!" shouted Rosalie. Shea pointed at another jar. "Blue!" said Shea. "Yellow!" said Rosalie. Mr. Castillo smiled. "Those are the primary colours."

Rosalie dipped her brush in the red paint. She made a big red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue paint. She touched the paper. "Look!" she cried. The circle turned purple. "Purple! I made purple!" Shea ran over to see. "Make more!" said Shea. Rosalie painted purple all over the paper.

At home time, Rosalie set her brush down in the paint cup. She wanted to hurry and show her father. "Wait," said Mr. Castillo. He showed her the sink. "Paintbrushes are washed with water and left to dry when painting is finished." Rosalie rinsed her brush in the cool water. She laid it on the rack to dry.

The next day, Rosalie ran back to the art room. Her brush was soft and clean. It was true! She picked it up fast. "My turn for yellow and red," she said. She painted a yellow sun. She added red on top. "Orange!" she yelled. "Orange like a pumpkin!" Shea clapped. Mr. Castillo gave her a fresh sheet of paper. Rosalie dipped her clean, soft brush and wrote her name at the top in orange paint.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your nose has two openings called nostrils.
story:
Jules stood in the kitchen. He was hungry. He wanted warm toast. Mom put bread in the toaster. Jules watched with his eyes. The bread popped up high. "Pop!" said Jules.

Then he heard a knock at the door. He used his ears. It was his friend Rhea. "Toast!" said Rhea. "I smell it with my nose." Jules sniffed too. The toast smelled warm and good. Mom gave them each a piece. Jules touched it with his fingers. The top was bumpy. He took a bite. It tasted sweet with jam.

"Rhea, how many openings does your nose have?" asked Jules. "I don't know," said Rhea. Mom said, "Those openings are called nostrils." Jules ran to the little mirror. He looked and looked. He counted one, two. "Two nostrils!" he said. "Me too!" said Rhea. Then they sniffed their toast at the same time. "I can smell with both," said Jules. They giggled and ate the last bite.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: You see colors with your eyes; you cannot tell a color by feeling it with your fingers.
story:
Grandma had a big soft bag. "Put your hand in," she said. "Do not peek. Tell me what you find."

Milo put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and smooth. "A ball!" he said. "A red ball!"

Grandma smiled. "Take it out and look."

Milo pulled out the ball. It was blue! He laughed. "I felt it was a ball. But my fingers did not know the color."

Wade and Miraal were there too. They wanted a turn. Wade put his hand in. "A spoon! A yellow spoon!" He looked. The spoon was red. "My fingers cannot see," he said.

Miraal had a turn next. She felt something small and smooth. "A car! A blue car!" She peeked in the bag. "No, it is green!"

"Close your eyes," said Milo. "Now look at the ball. What color is it?" Miraal opened her eyes. "Blue. I see blue with my eyes."

Grandma yawned. She looked tired. "Time for my nap," she said. The children hurried to be quiet.

Milo held the bag shut. "No peeking," he whispered. "You have to look. Looking is how you see."

Miraal put her hand back in. "I feel it! It is a yellow duck." She pulled it out fast.

It was yellow! She jumped up and down. "I guessed it! My eyes and my hands both helped me!"
